https://www.dw.com/en/how-drought-threat.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5IPa0 Lights are turned off at Budapest landmarks — like the parliament building — to save energy during the power crisis Image: Bernadett Szabo/REUTERS Advertisement Riverbeds reduced to tiny streams, asphalt melting like butter, dried-up fields — these are currently the images of drought in Central and Southeastern Europe. The record-breaking lack of rainfall in recent months and this summer's heatwaves have caused severe damage to the region's economy and infrastructure. In the agriculture sector, it has been clear for some time that harvests in Southeastern Europe, especially maize and sunflower crops, will be significantly below average. The heatwaves are also repeatedly disrupting road, rail and, above all, shipping transport. But, most importantly, the drought has triggered an unprecedented crisis in electricity generation in several Central and Southeastern European countries, forcing companies to halt production due to the historically low water level of the Danube. Hungary and Romania are currently most affected by the energy crisis. Other countries bordering the Danube — Austria , Slovakia , Serbia and Bulgaria — are also suffering from low water levels, although not as severely as Hungary and Romania. DW outlines the situation in each country and explains why, despite facing similar weather conditions, some are more severely affected than others. Hungary: Most severe energy crisis in decades No country in the region is currently as severely affected by drought and heat as Hungary. For months, there has been little or no rainfall in large parts of the country. On Wednesday, temperatures reached 43 degrees Celsius (109.4 degrees Fahrenheit) in the capital Budapest , and exceeded 40 degrees in many places across the country. Due to the record-low water levels of the Danube, the Paks nuclear power plant south of Budapest had to largely shut down operations, as there is no longer sufficent cooling water available and the temperature of the Danube water is too high. The plant is currently operating at around 12% of its capacity. If Danube water levels continue to drop, the plant will have to be shut down completely. Due to the energy crisis, the Hungarian government has been urging large energy consumers to conserve electricity. As a result, several car manufacturers, including Audi Gyor, oil and gas company MOL and other large companies have scaled back production. Hungary's energy crisis — the worst in decades — is so severe because of the country's unfavorable energy mix. Paks generates around 50% of the electricity produced in Hungary and about one-third of the electricity consumed. Although Hungary has significant solar energy capacity, it lacks storage facilities, has too few modern gas-fired power plants and very little wind or hydropower capacity. In Prahovo (eastern Serbia), the Danube's low water level has revealed the remains of a German WW II warship Image: Darko Vojinovic/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance Even if the Danube water levels rise significantly again, the Paks nuclear power plant cannot simply be brought back online quickly — the process takes a considerable amount of time. Therefore, Hungary's energy crisis will continue for at least several more weeks, during which the country will have to import electricity at high prices. In response to the crisis, the new government under Peter Magyar has announced a comprehensive review of Hungary's energy development strategy. Romania: Blasting rocks to redirect water Romania is experiencing a similar, though somewhat less severe, energy crisis. The Cernavoda nuclear power plant, also located on the Danube in the southeast of the country, produces roughly one-fifth of Romania's electricity. Due to the river's exceptionally low water level, one of the plant's two 700-megawatt reactors was taken offline last week. Southwest of the Cernavoda plant, Romanian authorities blasted a rock formation this week to divert more water into the Danube's eastern branch, where the nuclear plant is located. In addition, dozens of tons of rock were dumped into the river to channel more water into that branch. Romania's navy carried out a controlled blast of submerged rocks to allow more water to flow into the eastern branch of the Danube Image: Vadim Ghirda/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance Romania has a relatively balanced energy mix consisting of hydropower, nuclear energy, natural gas, coal and wind power. However, because hydropower accounts for around one-fifth of the country's electricity generation — primarily through the Iron Gate hydroelectric plant on the Danube — Romania is particularly vulnerable to droughts such as the current one. Due to the energy crisis, several major companies, including Dacia and Ford Romania, have scaled back production. The government has announced that it would, if necessary, issue a decree ordering large factories to suspend production. Romania is also among the Southeastern European countries most affected by aridification — the long-term climatic process through which regions become increasingly dry — and desertification, as soils gradually become barren and take on desert-like characteristics. Serbia: An unfavorable energy mix Serbia, too, is suffering badly from drought and the Danube's low water level. Its energy mix is similarly ill-suited to prolonged dry periods. Around 65% of its electricity is generated by coal-fired power plants, while about 25% comes from hydropower. The two Iron Gate hydropower plants are currently generating only a fraction of their average electricity output. The coal-fired power plants Kostolac A and B east of Belgrade , which rely on Danube water for cooling, have also had to cut back production. In Hungary, dropping water levels of the Danube threaten the complete shutdown of the Paks nuclear power plant Image: David Balogh/Xinhua/IMAGO Serbia relies heavily on the Danube as a transport route for coal and petrochemical products. However, due to the low water level, cargo vessels can currently only carry a fraction of their normal loads. Nonetheless, the energy crisis has so far not been so severe that large industrial plants have had to scale back production. Slovakia, Austria less affected In Slovakia, some 60% of electricity is generated by nuclear power plants, with another 20% by hydropower. Unlike Hungary and Romania, Slovakia's two nuclear power plants, Bohunice and Mochovce, are located on smaller rivers and use cooling towers rather than once-through cooling systems. Once-through cooling requires large quantities of river water that are drawn from the river and then channeled back to it at a higher temperature. In contrast, cooling towers recirculate water in a closed system, releasing heat mainly through evaporation. As a result, Slovakia's nuclear plants require much less river water and are therefore less affected by the current drought. In comparison, Slovakia's Gabcikovo hydropower on the Danube has been significantly affected by the low water level. At present, only one of its eight turbines is in operation. Electricity generation in Gabcikovo, however, is only about 12% lower compared to the same time last year. So far, Slovakia has not experienced any major industrial production stoppages. Austria, which generates around 60% of its electricity from hydropower, has also been less severely affected than Hungary. One reason is that part of Austria's hydropower capacity comes from storage and pumped-storage plants rather than run-of-river facilities. Run-of-river plants depend directly on the volume of water flowing through rivers, whereas storage and pumped-storage plants can generate electricity using water stored in reservoirs when needed, making them less vulnerable during prolonged heatwaves and droughts. In addition, Austria generates some 30% of its electricity from other renewable energy sources. Cargo ships anchor near Petrovaradin, Serbia, on the Danube amid extremely low levels of water following an extended period of drought Image: Darko Vojinovic/AP Photo/picture alliance Bulgaria: Large battery storage capacity Unlike in neighboring Romania, drought and heat are not yet causing an energy crisis in Bulgaria. The country generates up to 40% of its energy through the Kozloduy nuclear power plant, which is also located on the Danube. Its cooling system, however, is better designed to operate under low-water conditions than those of Hungary's Paks plant and Cernavoda in Romania. As a result, it is currently operating at almost full capacity. At the same time, Bulgaria depends only marginally on hydropower and has, in recent years, considerably expanded its solar and wind energy capacity. The biggest difference to all the other countries lies in Bulgaria's large-scale battery storage facilities. The country currently has storage systems with a capacity of 3.4 gigawatts and a storage capacity of 8.6 gigawatt-hours. This storage capacity corresponds to 16% of the country's total installed power generation capacity — a figure unmatched by any other country in the world. These storage facilities enable Bulgaria to balance supply shortages and peak demand, without relying on expensive imports. At the same time, the country is developing into a regional market leader in new energy concepts and as a hub for power grid stabilization and greater price stability in the electricity market. https://www.rbth.com/history/328985-harb.text: 8 mind-blowing facts about Harbin, the Chinese city built by Russians Go back 150 years and the area along the Songhua River was but a collection of rural settlements. Fast-forward to modern-day Harbin, and you’ll find 12 million Chinese citizens going about their lives amidst an architectural backdrop of Tsarist grandeur. The reason? Harbin is a city of perpetual re-invention and chaos. Now China’s 8 th largest urban area, current residents work on the skeleton of a village built in the early 20 th century by enterprising Russians in search of prosperity, and who tried to recreate their homeland. Today, the city is practically devoid of Russians (except a few expats), but Harbin’s history once was home to some of the Motherland’s brightest entrepreneurs, most vulnerable refugees, and its most scheming extremists. Here’s the lowdown on the city’s rich heritage. The first thing in Harbin was the train station. As the first Trans-Siberian trains made successful eastward voyages in 1896, Tsar Nicholas II’s ambitious Finance Minister, Count Sergei Witte, wasted no time in subsidizing another route: the Chinese Eastern Railway. Central to his grand plan was the newly-formed city of Harbin, which he hoped would link Baikal with Vladivostok, and then have southern routes through China. After officially acquiring town status in 1898, the area quickly became northeast China’s most buzzing metropolis, and by 1917 it was home to over 100,000 people (around 40,000 of whom were Russian). As very few had been born in the city, Harbin was an expat paradise. Count Witte was keen to make anyone looking at the Harbin skyline know who was boss. The result? St. Sophia Orthodox Cathedral (opened 1907) Volga Manor The European-style High St. in Daoli On the right: Lungmen Grand Hotel (opened in 1901) Long before the Jewish Autonomous Oblast existed, many of Russia’s Jews flocked eastwards to Harbin to escape persecution and start new lives. Since Alexander III and (to a lesser extent) Nicholas II were under the influence of their ultra-conservative childhood tutor, Konstantin Pobedonostsev, the prospect of deportations, education quotas, disenfranchisement, and even pogroms made an eastward move more tempting to Jews. By 1913, it is estimated that around 5,000 Russian Jews lived in Harbin, with this number rising to around 20,000 by 1920. Of Harbin’s Jewish legacy only two synagogues remain: one built in 1909; another in 1921; and also a large Jewish cemetery. Jewish cemetery in Harbin Although most White émigrés fled to Paris, Berlin and Prague, Harbin’s role in welcoming those persecuted by the Bolsheviks is often overlooked by historians. In a way, it makes perfect sense: starting in 1917 Harbin welcomed pro-Tsarist traders and bureaucrats. With White factions clearly taking note of this, the city’s Russian population skyrocketed from 40,000 to around 120,000 over the course of the Civil War. Although these White émigrés were mostly left stateless after 1922, their community briefly thrived in Harbin through the establishment of a Russian educational system and Russian-language media. In the 1930s, many in Harbin’s Russian community embraced fascism, mostly as an attempt to form an anti-Bolshevik Asian front with Emperor Hirohito’s Japan. The Russian Fascist Party’s most successful period was under the leadership of Konstantin Rodzaevsky, who claimed to have 20,000 members. Gladly agreeing to an alliance with Imperial Japan, Rodzaevsky’s platform called for liquidation of the Jews, re-establishing the influence of the Orthodox Church, and building a corporatist economic system along Italian lines. As a result of the RFP’s increasing power, as well as a lack of protection from the Japanese government following its annexation of Manchuria in 1931, the city’s Jewish population fell from 13,000 in 1931 to 5,000 by 1935. But things were about to become far more gruesome. The ruins of Unit 731 While officially labelled an “epidemic prevention and water supply unit,” and located just 24 km south of Harbin, Unit 731 in fact was responsible for some of the most brutal war crimes ever committed. Established in 1935 by the Japanese military, Unit 731 ran a facility for live human experimentation that even horror movies couldn’t imagine. Only in 1984 was it revealed that the Japanese subjected prisoners to live dissections, frostbite, starvation, as well as injecting them with the plague. Russians in Harbin were also targeted by the Japanese, and it's estimated that around 30 percent of the 3,000-12,000 victims of Unit 731 were Russian. Most set a 5 p.m. curfew for their children to prevent them being taken by Japanese police. Following the USSR’s sale of the Chinese Eastern Railway to Japan in 1935, as well as due to the random disappearance of people from the streets (taken by Unit 731), most Harbin Russians naturally wanted to leave. By the late 1930s the number of local Russians had fallen to around 30,000. Those who had chosen Soviet citizenship, and who had their property confiscated by the Japanese, chose to return to the USSR. Ironically, over 48,000 of them were arrested as “Japanese spies” during the Great Purge of 1936-38. When the Soviet army took the city in August 1945, many remaining residents met a similar fate: those deemed to have had any previous cooperation with the White Army, the Japanese, or the Russian Fascist Party were immediately rounded up and sent to the GULAG. Most remaining Russians in Harbin were repatriated to the Soviet Union, and in the Chinese census of 1964 just 450 Russians were counted in the city. The final two Harbin Russians died in the 1980s. A visitor of the ethnographic project "A Russian Village on Sun Island Near Harbin." Harbin’s historic Russian architecture is losing out to modern Chinese construction, but locals are fighting back. When there was talk about destroying the city’s iconic 1920s Qihong Bridge, a local movement fought to have it classified as “an immovable cultural relic.” When the Harbin Ice Festival comes to the city every year, the organizers make sure that an Ice Kremlin is built. One of the city’s historic restaurants, Lucia, has also preserved its unique Imperial Russian interior. https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text: Redevelopment of the Temple Quarter of Bristol including the Sloane Robinson Building, an addition to the University of Bristol. Photograph: Adrian Sherratt/The Guardian View image in fullscreen Redevelopment of the Temple Quarter of Bristol including the Sloane Robinson Building, an addition to the University of Bristol. Photograph: Adrian Sherratt/The Guardian Bristol ‘Gigantic spaceship’: University of Bristol’s flagship £500m campus opens Temple Quarter Enterprise Campus near to station will make it easier for students and staff to commute Steven Morris Sun 6 Sep 2026 19.01 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Not so long ago, the first impression for visitors arriving by train to Bristol’s main railway station was a derelict building described by David Cameron as looking like the entrance to a war zone. On Monday, a shiny new University of Bristol campus on the site of that crumbling Royal Mail sorting office next door to Temple Meads is opening its doors to students, teachers and members of the public. The proximity of the Temple Quarter Enterprise Campus (TQEC) to the station should make it easier for students and staff who cannot afford Bristol’s expensive property and rental market to commute, and for business and research partners from all across the country to attend meetings. The campus is also designed to be “porous”, with many areas completely open to the public, turning it into a front door to the university for Bristolians in a way that its grand buildings high on the hill in the leafy Clifton area never have been. View image in fullscreen The former Bristol Royal Mail sorting office next to Bristol Temple Meads train station was demolished in 2019. Photograph: Ben Birchall/PA The £500m campus is a major part of one of the UK’s biggest regeneration schemes, Bristol Temple Quarter , which is to bring thousands of new homes, work spaces and health and education centres to one of the city’s – and England’s – most deprived neighbourhoods. The scheme is so important to Labour locally and nationally that it got a mention in Andy Burnham’s first prime minister’s questions . Speaking in a garden space in TQEC almost directly above Temple Meads’ platform 15, Judith Squires, deputy vice chancellor and university lead for the TQEC, said the new site put the university “front and centre” in the city. “We think it opens up lots of opportunities that we haven’t yet explored,” she said. “One of them will be for students who commute to Bristol, which I think may become an increasingly important trend given that rent is such an expensive cost. Living at home is becoming an increasing option for students. “It also means that it’s very accessible for a lot of our staff who can commute in, but also for our industrial partners who will be coming to do research and collaboration in the building.” View image in fullscreen The Sloane Robinson building is the £241m centrepiece of the University of Bristol’s Temple Quarter campus. Photograph: Adrian Sherratt/The Guardian The site will be a hub for teaching and research across areas including business, innovation, digital engineering, artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, advanced telecommunications and quantum technologies. It features a rare example of a circular lecture theatre. When the Guardian visited, an actor and voice coach from Bristol Old Vic theatre was showing lecturers how to best use the space. But the university is keen to emphasise that it is is not just for academic types to use, but for all of Bristol’s citizens. A new entrance from the station to the campus has been created, and new footpaths and cycleways added. Spaces aimed at citizens include the Bristol Rooms and the Story Exchange on the ground floor, which are designed to bring academics and students together with business, public sector and community organisations. Sessions on topics important to Bristolians, such as health inequalities, reparative justice and the climate crisis, have already been organised. View image in fullscreen The Sloane Robinson building is named after a foundation set up by the former Bristol University student Hugh Sloane. Photograph: Adrian Sherratt/The Guardian Members of the public are to be allowed more casual access to the campus. They will be able to have a coffee on the campus, plug in a laptop and work or use it as a meeting spot. Squires said: “We wanted to make it a porous place so that people can feel it is a space for them, designed with them in mind. It’s really great to have such an accessible front door to the university where everybody can find it, so we don’t feel so cut off from the city. I think it positions us physically and symbolically in a different way with the city.” The main building has cost £241m and is named the Sloane Robinson building, after a foundation set up by the former Bristol University student and hedge fund manager Hugh Sloane, which donated £20m. The West of England Combined Authority (WECA) has invested £35m into the campus and £25m into the station entrance and new paths. The university has snapped up other parcels of land nearby so it can expand the campus in the coming years, taking the cost of the campus up to £500m. Behind the Sloane Robinson building, work on the wider Bristol Temple Quarter project is under way in the St Philip’s Marsh area of the city, currently a place of factories, waste disposal sites and Bristol’s fruit market. View image in fullscreen Members of the public will be able to have a coffee on the campus, plug in a laptop and work or use it as a meeting spot. Photograph: Adrian Sherratt/The Guardian Though the new quarter will be 30 years in the making, workers in hi-vis are preparing the way for new homes, shops, community spaces. A bridge is to be built from TQEC to link to it. Helen Godwin, the mayor of the West of England, said the opening of the campus was a major milestone for Bristol. “Our investment in Bristol Temple Quarter will unlock a giant leap forward for the West of England,” she said. Martin Booth, editor of the independent magazine and website Bristol 24/7 and author of 111 Places That You Shouldn’t Miss in Bristol , said the new site looked as if a “gigantic spaceship” had crash-landed next to the station. “But it is a manifestation of the university’s efforts to be a more visible part of our city – not just in their privileged position on top of a hill in Clifton,” he said. https://cyprus-mail.com/2026/10/15/eu-le.text: The European Union began a packed summit on Thursday that quickly underscored wrangles over how to tame soaring energy prices, design a budget to keep the bloc competitive and curb surging exports from China that are blamed for job losses. The leaders from the EU’s 27 members met in Brussels on the back of securing an agreement with Beijing to limit imports of hybrid cars from China, a first step towards cutting a goods trade deficit that hit €360 billion in 2025. The summit takes place at a time of heightened economic anxiety, with fuel price spikes since the Iran war putting cash-strapped governments on the back foot, companies struggling and Europe wanting to shore up its defences and support Ukraine. The clock is also ticking on a series of elections in Europe over the coming months including in France in April, which could propel French far-right leader Marine Le Pen to the presidency vowing to slash her country’s contribution to the EU budget. Slumping in the polls at home, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz told reporters that positions were still far apart on the budget, which has pitted net contributors such as Germany against net beneficiaries. The latest proposal would safeguard subsidies for farmers and regions, which critics say sucks money away from more urgent areas to keep up with the US and China. “We are, therefore, facing very, very difficult negotiations,” Merz said. MERZ SAYS FROZEN RUSSIAN ASSETS MUST STAY IN EUROPE Merz also gave a pointed rebuff to a proposal by the United States, reported in the Financial Times, for European countries to unfreeze some Russian sovereign assets immobilised after the invasion of Ukraine. The idea would be to transfer them to a vehicle overseen by Washington in an attempt to revive peace talks, the FT reported, citing people briefed on the matter. “These are assets that are frozen in Europe, and they should remain frozen in Europe. This is our affair, and we are the ones who decide on it,” Merz said. While France is also a net contributor to the EU budget, its officials warned that a blunt focus on spending cuts would be counterproductive, hobbling measures that were also intended to make the bloc more competitive. “We can clearly see that cuts alone cannot resolve the equation,” one official said. Draft conclusions from the summit indicate leaders want the Commission to continue talks with Beijing, while also making full use of EU trade defence measures and adding new trade instruments to protect the bloc further. “These imbalances are not limited to one sector. We don’t have much time because every month that goes by, thousands of jobs are lost,” said a senior EU diplomat. Beijing has said that hyping up the issue of economic imbalances is an excuse to promote protectionism and exert pressure on and restrict China. “We don’t have enough measures to counter unfair practices, we have also not invested enough in our own competitiveness and innovation, the new EU budget will need to be equipped for that,” Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten told reporters. GERMANY’S U-TURN ON CHINA IMPORTS Franco-German proposals released last week are also likely to be the focus of discussions. The EU’s two largest economies said there was an urgent need for measures to deal with imports of chemicals and PET — the plastic widely used in packaging — and called for measures to retaliate quickly against countries that harm the bloc. The paper marks a sharp turn for Germany, which only two years ago was the most vocal critic of EU anti-subsidy tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles. Several EU countries have also put high energy prices on the agenda. One area of contention is the wish by countries including the Czech Republic and Italy to weaken or suspend the EU Emissions Trading System, a regulation forcing power plants and industries to buy CO2 permits when they pollute. The prime ministers of Finland, Sweden and Denmark hit back in a letter praising the system as a driver of energy security by helping Europe reduce reliance on imported fossil fuels. They warned “any weakening” would hinder investment in clean industries. One of Friday’s main topics will be the challenges facing Ukraine, with President Volodymyr Zelenskiy due to attend at a time when Kyiv is at loggerheads with the US over intelligence sharing while missiles and drones hammer Ukrainian cities. Leaders are expected to discuss Ukraine’s funding needs for 2027, with Latvia’s Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs comparing the cost to each citizen of the price of a beer. “It is one beer less for one European a year. We can afford that. But Ukraine needs it now,” he said.
